On this page

Layered sphere: the transfer matrices, symbolically ​

The whole page as one script

Every block of this page, in order, is scripts/69_layered_sphere_symbolic.jl. From a clone of the repository, julia --project=docs -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()' once, then julia scripts/69_layered_sphere_symbolic.jl, runs it end to end.

Before this page

The theory page Layered sphere — bulk + shear recurrences and imperfect interfaces states the recurrences of an n-layer sphere. This page derives them with TensND's symbolic differential operators: the transfer matrices of Hervé and Zaoui (1993), their extension to imperfect interfaces (Hervé-Luanco, 2014), and the order of the products when the moduli are operators. The cylinder has its own page, Layered cylinder: the transfer relations, symbolically.

A LayeredSphere is a core and concentric isotropic shells in an infinite isotropic matrix, under a remote uniform strain. That strain splits into a spherical part and a deviatoric one, and the displacement of each layer is, for each part, a combination of a few elementary fields, the modes. The method is to find the modes, to write what an interface transmits, and to chain the layers.

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization
using TensND
using SymPyPythonCall
using LinearAlgebra

1. An isotropic layer in spherical coordinates ​

TensND orders the spherical coordinates , being the colatitude. The stiffness of a layer is     .

julia
Sph = coorsys_spherical()
θ, φ, r = get_coords(Sph)
𝐞ᶿ, 𝐞ᵠ, 𝐞ʳ = unitvec(Sph)
k, μ = symbols("k mu", positive = true)
ℂ = TensISO{3}(3k, 2μ)
stress(u) = ℂ ⊡ symgrad(u, Sph)
equilibrium(u) = divergence(stress(u), Sph)

2. Spherical part: the matrices and ​

Under a remote spherical strain the displacement is radial,   , and equilibrium reduces to

julia
f = SymFunction("f", real = true)
simplify((equilibrium(f(r) * 𝐞ʳ) ⋅ 𝐞ʳ) / (3k + 4μ))

an Euler equation of solutions and :   . The quantities continuous across a perfect interface are the displacement and the radial stress; they depend linearly on :

julia
A, B = symbols("A B", real = true)
u_bulk = A * r + B / r^2
σrr_bulk = simplify((stress(u_bulk * 𝐞ʳ) ⋅ 𝐞ʳ) ⋅ 𝐞ʳ)
J(ρ, kk, μμ) = [ρ 1 / ρ^2; 3kk -4μμ / ρ^3]
@assert iszero(simplify(σrr_bulk - (J(r, k, μ) * [A, B])[2]))
J(r, k, μ)

Continuity at the radius between a layer and the next one is    , so the amplitudes are carried by the matrix

julia
k₁, μ₁, k₂, μ₂, R = symbols("k_1 mu_1 k_2 mu_2 R", positive = true)
N = simplify.(inv(J(R, k₂, μ₂)) * J(R, k₁, μ₁))

The product of these matrices from the core (where  ) to the matrix gives every amplitude per unit core amplitude; the remote strain fixes the latter. For one sphere in a matrix, the strain of the sphere per unit remote strain is the classical

julia
simplify(1 / N[1, 1])

The package propagates the state rather than the amplitudes, which keeps an incompressible layer ( ) regular; the transfer across a layer is the same product in the other order:

julia
const LS = MeanFieldHomogenization.LayeredSpheres
r₁, r₂ = symbols("r_1 r_2", positive = true)
@assert all(iszero, simplify.(LS._bulk_layer_transfer(r₂, r₁, k, μ) .- J(r₂, k, μ) * inv(J(r₁, k, μ))))

3. Deviatoric part: the matrices and ​

Every deviatoric strain is a sum of rotated copies of the axisymmetric one      , whose displacement is carried by the Legendre polynomial :       , the prime being the derivative in . With power laws   ,   :

julia
s, a, b = symbols("s a b", real = true)
P₂ = (3cos(θ)^2 - 1) / 2
u_dev(U, W) = U * P₂ * 𝐞ʳ + W * diff(P₂, θ) * 𝐞ᶿ
eq = equilibrium(u_dev(a * r^s, b * r^s))
E₁ = simplify((eq ⋅ 𝐞ʳ) / (r^(s - 2) * P₂))
E₂ = simplify((eq ⋅ 𝐞ᶿ) / (r^(s - 2) * diff(P₂, θ)))
system = [diff(E₁, a) diff(E₁, b); diff(E₂, a) diff(E₂, b)]
factor(det(system))

Four modes,    , of shapes

julia
shapes = [simplify.(subs.(system, s => q).nullspace()[1]') for q in (1, 3, -4, -2)]
4-element Vector{Matrix{SymPyCore.Sym{PythonCall.Py}}}:
 [2 1]
 [6*(3*k - 2*mu)/(15*k + 11*mu) 1]
 [-3 1]
 [3*k/mu + 3 1]

The first one is the uniform strain. With the amplitudes and the normalization of Christensen and Lo (1979),

julia
a, b, c, d = symbols("a b c d", real = true)
x = k / μ
U = 2r * a + 6(3x - 2) * r^3 * b + 3c / r^4 + 3(x + 1) * d / r^2
W = r * a + (15x + 11) * r^3 * b - c / r^4 + d / r^2
@assert all(iszero, simplify.(TensND.canonical_components(equilibrium(u_dev(U, W)))))

The traction has the same angular shapes,   and  ; its radial functions are read at one angle:

julia
coefficient(e, g) = factor(simplify(subs(e, θ => PI / 3) / subs(g, θ => PI / 3)))
σ = stress(u_dev(U, W))
state = [U, W, coefficient((σ ⋅ 𝐞ʳ) ⋅ 𝐞ʳ, P₂), coefficient((σ ⋅ 𝐞ʳ) ⋅ 𝐞ᶿ, diff(P₂, θ))]
L = simplify.([diff(q, amp) for q in state, amp in (a, b, c, d)])

maps the amplitudes to the state (radial functions of the displacement and of the traction), and   carries the amplitudes across a perfect interface, as does for the spherical part. The package uses the same modes, the second and the fourth scaled by    so that they stay finite for an incompressible layer:

julia
sμ = μ / (k + μ)
L_pkg = LS._shear_M_matrix(r, k, μ)
@assert all(iszero, simplify.(L_pkg .- L * Diagonal([1, sμ, 1, sμ])))

4. Imperfect interfaces ​

Across an imperfect interface the state is not continuous: it is multiplied by a jump matrix , and the transfer of the amplitudes becomes    (resp.   ).

A spring opens in proportion to the traction, which stays continuous:  ,  . The jump matrices carry and above the diagonal:

julia
kn, kt = symbols("k_n k_t", positive = true)
LS._bulk_interface_T(SpringInterface(kn, kt), k, μ, R)

julia
LS._shear_interface_T(SpringInterface(kn, kt), k, μ, R)

A membrane keeps the displacement continuous and carries a surface stress    of the strain in the tangent plane; its equilibrium makes the traction jump,    . The surface stress, read on the sphere and extended in the radial direction as a homogeneous function of degree zero, has the surface divergence as its divergence on  :

julia
λs, μs = symbols("lambda_s mu_s", positive = true)
𝟏 = TensISO{3}(Sym(1))
Pᵗ = 𝟏 - 𝐞ʳ ⊗ 𝐞ʳ
function traction_jump(u)
    εs = Pᵗ ⋅ symgrad(u, Sph) ⋅ Pᵗ
    σs = tsubs(λs * tr(εs) * Pᵗ + 2μs * εs, r => R)
    return -tsubs(divergence(σs, Sph), r => R)
end
u₀, U₀, W₀ = symbols("u_0 U_0 W_0", real = true)
jump_bulk = simplify(traction_jump(u₀ * 𝐞ʳ) ⋅ 𝐞ʳ)

julia
t = traction_jump(u_dev(U₀, W₀))
jump_dev = (coefficient(t ⋅ 𝐞ʳ, P₂), coefficient(t ⋅ 𝐞ᶿ, diff(P₂, θ)))
(4*(U_0 - 3*W_0)*(lambda_s + mu_s)/R^2, -2*(U_0*lambda_s + U_0*mu_s - 3*W_0*lambda_s - 5*W_0*mu_s)/R^2)

With   , these are the entries of the jump matrices of MembraneInterface:

julia
κs = λs + μs
Tb = LS._bulk_interface_T(MembraneInterface(κs, μs), k, μ, R)
Td = LS._shear_interface_T(MembraneInterface(κs, μs), k, μ, R)
@assert iszero(simplify(Tb[2, 1] * u₀ - jump_bulk))
@assert all(iszero, simplify.((Td * [U₀, W₀, 0, 0])[3:4] .- collect(jump_dev)))
Td

In conduction the temperature of the mode is   . A Kapitza resistance makes it jump,    , the flux being continuous; a conducting surface carries the flux   , whose surface divergence the normal flux balances,   :

julia
ks, T₀ = symbols("k_s T_0", positive = true)
simplify(-subs(divergence(-ks * (Pᵗ ⋅ grad(T₀ * cos(θ), Sph)), Sph), r => R) / cos(θ))

julia
LS._cond_interface_T(SurfaceConductiveInterface(ks), k, R)

5. Two closed forms ​

A grain bonded to its matrix by a spring answers a pressure as a grain of bulk modulus  :

julia
k₀, μ₀ = symbols("k_0 mu_0", positive = true)
grain = LayeredSphere((R,), (TensISO{3}(3k₁, 2μ₁),); interfaces = (SpringInterface(kn, kt),))
α = TensND.get_data(gradient_gradient_concentration(grain, TensISO{3}(3k₀, 2μ₀), TensISO{3}(3k₀, 2μ₀)))[1]
@assert iszero(simplify(α - (3k₀ + 4μ₀) / (3k₁ / (1 + 3k₁ / (kn * R)) + 4μ₀)))
factor(simplify(α))

A core of radius coated up to the radius 1 by answers a pressure as a homogeneous sphere whose bulk modulus is that of the composite-sphere model:

julia
ρ = symbols("a", positive = true)
coated = LayeredSphere((ρ, Sym(1)), (TensISO{3}(3k₁, 2μ₁), TensISO{3}(3k₂, 2μ₂)))
states, outer = LS._bulk_state_seq(coated, k₂, μ₂)
k_eff = factor(simplify(outer[2] / (3 * outer[1])))

julia
cf = ρ^3
@assert iszero(simplify(k_eff - (k₂ + cf * (k₁ - k₂) * (3k₂ + 4μ₂) / (3k₂ + 4μ₂ + 3 * (1 - cf) * (k₁ - k₂)))))

6. Moduli that do not commute ​

In aging linear viscoelasticity and are Volterra operators and the amplitudes are histories. The matrices above keep their form, each product read in the order the mechanics gives: a modulus acts on the left of the strain it multiplies. Two places need care.

The transfer across an interface. With non-commuting symbols, the continuity of the radial stress and the opening of a spring of compliance at the radius give the amplitude of the outer layer:

julia
K₁, M₁, K₂, M₂, Sₙ, A₁, B₁ = symbols("K_1 M_1 K_2 M_2 S_n A_1 B_1", commutative = false)
σ⁻ = 3K₁ * A₁ - 4M₁ * B₁ / R^3
u⁺ = R * A₁ + B₁ / R^2 + Sₙ * σ⁻
expand(σ⁻ + 4M₂ * u⁺ / R)                    # = (3K₂ + 4M₂) ∘ A₂

     

The factor of is      : outer shear modulus, then the compliance, then the inner bulk modulus, and the division by   is on the left. No other order is admissible.

The shapes of the deviatoric modes. Equilibrium is linear in the moduli, each one on the left of an amplitude: the two equations of a mode   ,    are obtained from the ones of section 3 by putting the moduli back on the left.

julia
K, Mo, αo, βo, bo, do_ = symbols("K M alpha beta b d", commutative = false)
operator_form(E, q) = expand(
    sum(
        subs(diff(E, mod, amp), s => q) * Op * H
            for (mod, Op) in ((k, K), (μ, Mo)), (amp, H) in ((a, αo), (b, βo))
    )
)
mode_equations(q) = (operator_form(E₁, q), operator_form(E₂, q))
mode_equations(3)
(10*K*alpha - 12*K*beta + 22*M*alpha/3 + 8*M*beta, 5*K*alpha - 6*K*beta + 11*M*alpha/3 + 4*M*beta)

The modes and of section 3, with read as   — the inverse on the left —, satisfy them identically:

julia
X = Mo^-1 * K
check(q, αe, βe) = [simplify(expand(Mo^-1 * subs(e, αo => αe, βo => βe))) for e in mode_equations(q)]
(check(3, 6(3X - 2) * bo, (15X + 11) * bo), check(-2, 3(X + 1) * do_, do_))
(SymPyCore.Sym{PythonCall.Py}[0, 0], SymPyCore.Sym{PythonCall.Py}[0, 0])

and with the other order,  , they do not:

julia
Xʳ = K * Mo^-1
check(3, 6(3Xʳ - 2) * bo, (15Xʳ + 11) * bo)

This is the form the aging recurrences of the package use: the ratio   applied on the left in the mode shapes, and the products of section 6 in the transfers. Their use is described in Aging viscoelasticity.
